title: Clergy, laity, religious (CCC 871–945)
hook: different callings in one people, equal in dignity

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Church as people, body and temple. Your line was three pictures. Did a church building remind you of them? Day one thousand eighty-one.

Tuesday morning at a parish. A retired nurse unlocks the food pantry and starts sorting cans. Down the hall, a sister in a plain habit is running a Bible study for new mothers. The pastor is in the office, on the phone with a family planning a funeral. A teenager is setting up chairs for confirmation class. A man who'll never set foot in the office is, at that moment, telling the truth at work when it would be easier not to. Which of them is the Church? The Catechism's answer is all of them, in different callings. Today's word is the name for the nurse, the teenager and the man at work.
screen: `A PANTRY, A STUDY, AN OFFICE.` → `A MAN AT WORK.` → `WHICH ONE IS THE CHURCH?`

segments.voice: The Catechism begins with what everyone shares. All the baptized, it says, share in Christ's work as priest, prophet and king, each in their own way. And then a strong line: among all the faithful there is a true equality of dignity and of action, because all are reborn in Christ. Paul says the same thing about gifts, in the Douay-Rheims: "there are diversities of ministries, but the same Lord." Different jobs. Same Lord. Same dignity. Then the Catechism names the callings. Clergy are those ordained, as bishops, priests and deacons, to teach, sanctify and lead in Christ's name. Religious are those who take vows of poverty, chastity and obedience in a community the Church recognizes: the sister running the Bible study. And the laity are everyone else among the faithful. That's how the Catechism defines them: all the faithful except those in holy orders and those in the religious state. It's a definition by what they aren't, but it doesn't stop there. The laity have their own calling, the Catechism says, a secular one. They seek God's kingdom by engaging in ordinary affairs, family, work, politics, culture, and ordering them toward God. The nurse sorting cans and the man telling the truth at work aren't helping the Church from outside. The Catechism says some people will hear the gospel only through them. Acts has an early picture of it: Priscilla and Aquila, a married couple who made tents, take a gifted preacher named Apollos aside and explain the way of God to him more fully. The Catechism also quotes Pope Pius the Twelfth saying of lay believers that they are the Church. So: different callings, no ranks of worth. A bishop, a sister and a bus driver stand before God with the same baptism.
screen: `ALL SHARE CHRIST'S WORK.` · `A TRUE EQUALITY OF DIGNITY.` · `CLERGY, RELIGIOUS, AND LAITY.` · `WHERE ONLY THEY CAN REACH.` · then, large: `DIVERSITIES OF MINISTRIES, BUT THE SAME LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a layperson who serves. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who gives their time to a church or a community without a collar or a title: the person who runs the food drive, teaches the class, plays the piano, visits the sick, keeps the books. Hold their face for a moment. Think of one specific thing they did that helped. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. If you don't, just let the thanks sit in you, and decide how you'll pass it on. The bell holds the time.
Laity. All the faithful who are not ordained or in religious life, called to bring the kingdom into family, work and public life, with an equal dignity. Today's word.
Your line: equal dignity. Today, actually tell that person thank you, with a text, a note, or a word at the door, and name the specific thing. Day one thousand eighty-one.

howItsDone: In Catholic parishes lay people serve as readers, catechists, musicians and parish council members, and Catholic teaching sees their everyday work and family life as their particular share in the Church's mission.
